title: Image and preimage
body: The image of an input value is the single output value yielded by the function rule, and the preimage of an output value is the set of input values for which the function rule yields that output value.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.2: "The image of an input value is the single output value yielded by the function rule. The preimage of an output value is the set of input values for which the function rule yields that output value." (also 1.12.A.5)

title: Rate of change at a point
body: The rate of change of a function at a point quantifies the rate at which output values would change were the input values to change at that point, and it can be approximated by average rates of change over small intervals containing the point, if such values exist.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.2: "The rate of change of a function at a point quantifies the rate at which output values would change were the input values to change at that point."

title: Concavity from changing average rates of change
body: When average rates of change over equal-length input-value intervals are increasing, the graph is concave up, and when they are decreasing, the graph is concave down.
ced_evidence: 1.3.B.3: "When the average rate of change over equal-length input-value intervals is increasing for all small-length intervals, the graph of the function is concave up." (also 1.1.B.3, 1.1.B.4, 1.4.A.5)

title: Sign of a rate of change
body: A positive rate of change means the two quantities increase or decrease together, and a negative rate of change means that as one quantity increases the other decreases.
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.2 and 1.2.B.3: "A positive rate of change indicates that as one quantity increases or decreases, the other quantity does the same." / "A negative rate of change indicates that as one quantity increases, the other decreases."

title: Polynomial function in standard form
body: p(x)=a_n x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+a_{n-2}x^{n-2}+\cdots+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0,\quad n \text{ a positive integer},\ a_n\neq 0
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1: "p(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + a_{n-2}x^{n-2} + ... + a_2x^2 + a_1x + a_0, where n is a positive integer, a_i is a real number ... and a_n is nonzero"

title: Extrema between zeros
body: Between every two distinct real zeros of a nonconstant polynomial function there must be at least one input value corresponding to a local maximum or local minimum.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.3: "Between every two distinct real zeros of a nonconstant polynomial function, there must be at least one input value corresponding to a local maximum or local minimum."

title: Even-degree polynomials and global extrema
body: A polynomial function of even degree has either a global maximum or a global minimum, and for a quadratic function that global extremum occurs at the vertex.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.4: "A polynomial function of even degree has either a global maximum or a global minimum."

title: Zeros as endpoints of inequality intervals
body: Real zeros of a polynomial can be endpoints of intervals satisfying polynomial inequalities, and for a rational function the real zeros of the numerator and denominator are endpoints or asymptotes for intervals satisfying r(x) ≥ 0 or r(x) ≤ 0.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3: "real zeros of a polynomial can be endpoints for intervals satisfying polynomial inequalities"; 1.8.A.2: "endpoints or asymptotes for intervals satisfying the rational function inequalities"

title: Multiplicity of a zero
body: If a linear factor (x - a) is repeated n times, the corresponding zero has multiplicity n, and a polynomial function of degree n has exactly n complex zeros when counting multiplicities.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.2: "If a linear factor ( x - a ) is repeated n times, the corresponding zero of the polynomial function has a multiplicity n."

title: End behavior limit notation for polynomials
ced_evidence: 1.6.A.1 and 1.6.A.2: "lim p(x) = ∞ or lim p(x) = -∞" as x → ∞ and as x → -∞; 1.6.A.3: degree and sign of the leading term determine end behavior

title: Factored form vs. standard form
body: Factored form readily provides information about real zeros, x-intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain, and range, while standard form can reveal information about end behavior.
ced_evidence: 1.11.A.1 and 1.11.A.2: "the factored form of a polynomial or rational function readily provides information about real zeros" / "The standard form ... can reveal information about end behaviors"

title: Location of a hole
body: \lim_{x\to c} r(x)=L \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{hole at } (c, L),\quad \text{where } \lim_{x\to c^-} r(x)=\lim_{x\to c^+} r(x)=\lim_{x\to c} r(x)=L
ced_evidence: 1.10.A.2: "the hole is located at the point with coordinates ( c , L ). The corresponding mathematical notation is lim r(x) = L"

title: Polynomial long division identity
ced_evidence: 1.11.B.1: "f can be rewritten as f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where q is the quotient, r is the remainder, and the degree of r is less than the degree of g"

title: Choosing a function type for a model
body: Match the function type to the pattern in the data or context, in the order the CED lists them.

items.label: Quadratic
items.meaning: Roughly linear rates of change, or data roughly symmetric with a unique maximum or minimum; area or two-dimensional contexts (1.13.A.2, 1.13.A.3).

items.label: Polynomial
items.meaning: Multiple real zeros or multiple maxima or minima (1.13.A.4).

items.label: Polynomial of degree n or less
items.meaning: Can model a graph of n + 1 points with distinct input values (1.13.A.6).

items.label: Piecewise-defined
items.meaning: Different characteristics over different, nonoverlapping domain intervals (1.13.A.7).

ced_evidence: 1.13.A.1–1.13.A.7: "Linear functions model data sets or aspects of contextual scenarios that demonstrate roughly constant rates of change."

title: Additive and multiplicative transformations
body: The four transformation forms of f and the effect each has on the graph of f.

items.label: g(x) = f(x) + k
items.meaning: Vertical translation of the graph of f by k units.

items.label: g(x) = f(x + h)
items.meaning: Horizontal translation of the graph of f by −h units.

items.label: g(x) = a·f(x), a ≠ 0
items.meaning: Vertical dilation by a factor of |a|; if a < 0, also a reflection over the x-axis.

items.label: g(x) = f(bx), b ≠ 0
items.meaning: Horizontal dilation by a factor of 1/|b|; if b < 0, also a reflection over the y-axis.

ced_evidence: 1.12.A.1–1.12.A.4: "g(x) = f(x + h) ... results in a horizontal translation of the graph of f by −h units"

title: Model assumptions and restrictions
body: The kinds of underlying assumptions and restrictions a function model may have.

items.label: Assumptions about what is consistent
items.meaning: A model may assume certain things stay consistent (1.13.B.1).

items.label: Assumptions about how quantities change together
items.meaning: A model may assume a particular way the quantities vary together (1.13.B.2).

items.label: Domain restrictions
items.meaning: Based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set (1.13.B.3).

items.label: Range restrictions
items.meaning: Such as rounding values, based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set (1.13.B.4).

ced_evidence: 1.13.B.1–1.13.B.4: "A model may require domain restrictions based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set."

title: Ways to construct a function model
body: The construction approaches the CED names for linear, quadratic, cubic, quartic, degree-n polynomial, and piecewise-defined models.

items.label: From identified restrictions
items.meaning: Build the model based on restrictions identified in a mathematical or contextual scenario (1.14.A.1).

items.label: Transformations of a parent function
items.meaning: Model a data set or scenario using transformations of the parent function (1.14.A.2).

items.label: Technology and regression
items.meaning: Use linear, quadratic, cubic, or quartic regression to model a data set (1.14.A.3).

items.label: Combined techniques for piecewise models
items.meaning: Construct a piecewise-defined model through a combination of modeling techniques (1.14.A.4).

ced_evidence: 1.14.A.1–1.14.A.4: "A model of a data set can be constructed using technology and regressions, including linear, quadratic, cubic, and quartic regressions."
